extracted.intended_audience: policymakers, advocates, journalists, and informed citizens concerned with national-security transparency and oversight
extracted.subtask_description: Policy guidance and recommended standards for improving transparency, reducing secret law, and strengthening oversight and accountability of classification and intelligence activities in the national-security context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law itself should never be secret
rubrics_metrics.description: The law itself should never be secret.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page argues that while operational details may sometimes be secret, the legal standards governing government conduct must be public. Excessive reliance on secret legal memos, classified court opinions, and unpublished regulations undermines democratic accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curtail classification of legal standards (no secret law)
rubrics_metrics.description: The president or Congress should adopt rules to sharply limit classification of the legal standards governing official conduct, whether in the form of agency rules and regulations, binding legal opinions issued by the Justice Department’s Office of Legal Counsel, international agreements that have the same legal force as treaties, or rulings of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly prohibits treating binding legal authorities (OLC opinions, FISC rulings, certain international agreements, agency regs) as classified material; recommends statutory or executive-branch rules to prevent such classification and to ensure those standards are publicly accessible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Change the incentives that lead to overclassification
rubrics_metrics.description: The executive order governing classification should be revised to require officials with classification authority to document their reasons for classifying information, and to require agencies to conduct spot audits for the purpose of identifying and holding accountable those who routinely overclassify.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two concrete mechanisms: (1) require documentation of the rationale for each classification decision, and (2) mandate agency spot audits to detect patterns of overclassification and enable accountability for officials who overuse classification authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require documentation for classification decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Require officials with classification authority to document their reasons for classifying information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Documentation creates an audit trail enabling review, oversight, and potential sanctions for improper classification; this is a specific reform proposed for the executive order on classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency spot audits and accountability for overclassifiers
rubrics_metrics.description: Require agencies to conduct spot audits for the purpose of identifying and holding accountable those who routinely overclassify.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spot audits are recommended as a systemic check to find and address patterns of unnecessary classification rather than treating classification as purely discretionary and unreviewed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Increase congressional oversight
rubrics_metrics.description: Solutions should include increased congressional oversight of national-security programs and classification practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Congressional oversight is presented as a key accountability mechanism alongside executive-branch reforms (e.g., reworking classification orders) to ensure transparency and lawful conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rework the executive order governing classification
rubrics_metrics.description: The executive order governing classification should be reworked to address overclassification and secrecy problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reworking the executive order is recommended to implement concrete fixes (documentation requirements, audits, limits on classifying legal standards) that structuralize better transparency practices across the executive branch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rethink and reform the intelligence establishment
rubrics_metrics.description: The intelligence establishment has grown too large, expensive, powerful, ineffective, and unaccountable; it is time to make intelligence collection more effective and more protective of individual rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calls for resizing/reshaping intelligence activities to improve effectiveness while embedding protections for civil liberties; implies criteria for evaluating intelligence programs include cost-effectiveness, necessity, proportionality, and accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Increase transparency in intelligence collection and policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Make intelligence collection and intelligence-related policy more transparent to the public and subject to greater scrutiny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Brennan Center advocates laying groundwork for a ‘more transparent and intelligent way to collect information,’ which implies greater disclosure about collection programs, oversight structures, and legal justifications to enable democratic evaluation and reform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency as prerequisite for accountability and democratic legitimacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Without transparency, there can be no accountability for government abuses and no way to ensure that government actions reflect the will of the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the normative rationale: secrecy prevents public and congressional scrutiny, enabling abuses and policies that can undermine civil liberties and national security; transparency is therefore a metric for legitimacy and effective oversight.
